Spheroidal harmonics and their re-expansion ​

See also

Theory: Spheroidal coordinates

Manual: Spheroidal harmonics · Charts and coordinate conversions

Tutorials: Changing the focal distance of spheroidal harmonics · The spheroid in spheroidal coordinates

The harmonic functions that separate in a spheroidal chart are products of associated Legendre functions of the two meridian coordinates. This page defines them, states how they are evaluated, and re-expresses a harmonic of one chart in the harmonics of a coaxial chart of another semi-focal distance, which is what a problem with two non-confocal spheroidal surfaces needs. The formulas are those of the appendix of Riccardi and Montheillet (1999), obtained here by another route, extended to the mixed prolate/oblate pairs and to the spherical limit, and completed by the domain of convergence of the exterior series.

The route uses no integral representation. Each spheroidal harmonic is first expanded in spherical solid harmonics from its values near the axis. A re-expansion is then an identity between the coefficients of these expansions, which is the coefficient identity of Gegenbauer's expansion of a Bessel function in Bessel functions of shifted order; the Bessel functions serve only as generating series.

The functions are the minimal solution. Scope of the proofs ​

Lemmas 1 to 6, the expansions of Lemmas 2 and 3 for both signs of , the coefficient identities of Theorems 1 and 2 for the four pairs, Theorem 2 as an identity at every point, Theorem 1 wherever its series converges locally uniformly, and the spherical limits are proved above. Neumann's integral, the moments used for the expansion of and the asymptotics of Theorem 3 (Szegő's for Jacobi polynomials, the ratio asymptotics of Legendre functions of large degree) are classical and quoted. The exact rate, the divergence outside and Theorem 3 in general are verified numerically only, in 256-bit arithmetic (unit roundoff about ): the functions and against the Neumann integral computed at 640 bits (relative difference below  ), the recurrence of the polynomials against the hypergeometric sum ( ), the interior identity for the four pairs ( , 1440 random cases per pair), the spherical limits ( ) and the exterior identity for six pairs ( ).

Relation to the formulas of Riccardi and Montheillet ​

Riccardi and Montheillet (1999) give the re-expansion for prolate and oblate charts of the same kind. The correspondence with the polynomials above is as follows.

The Bessel-function identity of their appendix, expressing   in the functions , has the bracket in its coefficient of index ; it equals , checked to for   and   (the residual is the cancellation in their sum over ). It is Lemma 5 with  , which accounts for the factor  .

For the exterior oblate expansion, written with   , the coefficient is   with  . It is the coefficient of the oblate-to-oblate pair above if their function equals up to a factor independent of . Their prolate rule, to multiply by  , agrees with of the prolate-to-prolate pair. For the interior expansions, with  , their coefficient reduces algebraically to of the oblate-to-oblate pair, with   steps, the argument and a bracket equal to by the identity above; their prolate factor     is the factor   of for   steps. This reduction was done by hand and not numerically. No discrepancy was found in the coefficients.

The correspondence fixes the normalization of the oblate functions and of the paper: its formulas are those above when they are   and  , the real functions of this page, up to factors independent of ; a factor that depends on , such as  , changes the coefficients. Their derivation starts from an integral representation of the harmonics by modified Bessel functions; the one above starts from the values of the harmonics on the axis, and adds the mixed pairs, the spherical limit and the domain of convergence of Theorem 3.

The change of chart of a point between two coaxial spheroidal charts is change_coords (see Changes of coordinates and Classical coordinate systems); the tutorial Changing the focal distance of spheroidal harmonics applies the formulas of this page with ProlateSpheroidalChart and OblateSpheroidalChart.
